nameStory: This hermit crab earned its 'hairy' name from the fuzzy bristles that cover its walking legs and claws, giving it a distinctly shaggy appearance underwater. The 'Western Atlantic' part of its name refers to its range along the eastern coast of North America, distinguishing it from Pacific hermit crab species.
description: The Western Atlantic Hairy Hermit Crab is a medium-sized hermit crab that makes its home in empty snail shells along New England's rocky shores. Like all hermit crabs, it has a soft, curved abdomen that it protects by backing into abandoned shells, which it carries around like a mobile home. Adults typically reach about 1-2 inches across when measured from claw to claw, with their borrowed shells often adding another inch or two to their overall size.

idTips.label: Hairy legs and claws
idTips.description: Dense, bristle-like hairs cover the walking legs and claws, feeling rough and fuzzy to the touch - much more pronounced than on smooth-legged hermit crab species

idTips.label: Reddish-orange coloration
idTips.description: Body and legs show warm reddish-orange to brick-red tones, often with darker banding on the legs that creates a striped appearance

idTips.label: Unequal claw size
idTips.description: Right claw is noticeably larger and more robust than the left, with the big claw feeling heavy and solid when the crab grips your finger

idTips.label: Shell preference
idTips.description: Often found in moon snail or whelk shells, which feel smooth and round, though they'll use periwinkle shells when smaller

idTips.label: Eye stalks
idTips.description: Long, mobile eye stalks that can retract quickly when threatened, with bright dark eyes that track movement

habitat: Look for these crabs in rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal areas along New England's coast, especially around tide pools and areas with coarse sand or gravel bottoms. They prefer areas with good shell availability and are often found near beds of blue mussels or areas where moon snails and whelks leave empty shells.

seasonality.spring: Crabs become more active as waters warm, often seen moving between tide pools during low tides. This is when they're most likely to be switching to new, larger shells as they grow.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most visible during low tides, actively foraging for food and shells. Best time for observation in shallow tide pools and rocky crevices.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper waters. May be seen clustering in protected areas as they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Move to deeper waters and become less active, rarely visible in intertidal zones except during unusually warm periods or very low tides.

funFact: When a hairy hermit crab outgrows its shell, it will actually line up with other hermit crabs in a 'housing chain' by size, where each crab waits for the largest one to upgrade to a new shell, then they all move up the chain into the next bigger shell like a bizarre real estate swap meet!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Long-claw Hermit Crab, but the hairy hermit's fuzzy legs are unmistakable once you know what to look for - if it feels bristly and rough, it's hairy; if it feels smooth, it's likely a long-claw. Remember: 'Hairy = bristly to touch.'
compareHints: Among New England's hermit crabs, the hairy hermit is the only one with distinctly fuzzy, bristled legs - its relatives like the Long-claw and Flat-clawed hermit crabs have smooth legs and claws. The Acadian hermit crab is much larger and found in deeper waters, while the Brown Banded hermit has smooth legs with distinctive brown and white striping.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's hermit crabs, the Long-claw is distinguished by its notably slender, elongated claws compared to the Flat-clawed Hermit Crab's broad, flattened pincers.

Among New England's hermit crabs, the flat-clawed hermit is unmistakable due to its shield-like claws - the long-claw hermit has thin, extended claws, while the Acadian hermit has more typical rounded pincers.
Compared to its close relative the Long-claw Hermit Crab, the Acadian hermit has a more robust build and prefers colder waters further north.

Unlike its relatives the Long-claw Hermit (which has elongated claws) and Flat-clawed Hermit (which has flattened, broad claws), the Brown Banded Hermit has proportionally normal-sized claws but sports those unmistakable brown leg bands.
